newsitem.title: USA: US job data seen robust, but not enough to tip Fed.
newsitem.headline: US job data seen robust, but not enough to tip Fed.

text.p: A drop in the U.S. jobless rate to its lowest level in almost 24 years will likely put new pressure on the Federal Reserve to tighten rates in July, former Fed officials and Wall Street experts said.
But those pundits cautioned that the labor market report released on Friday would not be viewed as the straw that breaks the camel's back.

"I would say that this morning's report maybe pushes the Fed a little closer to a tightening move in July. But it still is a very close call," Lyle Gramley, a former Federal Reserve governor, told Reuters.

"The economic numbers that come in between now and July, particularly the figures on retail sales for May and the ... orders for durable goods in May, are going to be decisive," said Gramley, now a consulting economist for the Mortgage Bankers Association.
The May retail sales report will be released on June 12 while durable goods orders will be announced on June 25.
The Fed's policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Market Committee, will next meet to deliberate on interest rate levels on July 1 and July 2.

Analysts said the most notable piece of information brought in by the employment report was a surprising drop to 4.8 percent in the jobless rate in May against a 4.9 percent rate in the previous month.
But although the numbers suggest labor markets remain tight, analysts said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has proved to Wall Street that he is a man who knows when to wait.
"The unemployment is low, very low ... and that puts more pressure on the Fed to think about tightening monetary policy," said William Dudley, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs and Co.

"But is it sufficient in itself to cause the Fed to tighten? Probably not. Greenspan has showed willingness to be patient when the unemployment is low as long as he doesn't see any inflation pressures," Dudley added.
Friday's employment report also added some extra pieces to the current economic puzzle.

Most notably, experts said a slower pace of job creation in May, when 138,000 positions were filled against a revised 323,000 reading in April, underlies the notion that the economy has been slowing substantially in the second quarter.
"(The employment report) confirms that we're going to have significantly slower growth in the second quarter," former Fed Governor Gramley said.

"Not only did we have a rather modest increase in payroll employment, but in the manufacturing sector aggregate hours worked went down, which suggested industrial production will probably be flat in the month of May," he added.
Analysts said the labor market report also suggested that the strong growth of the civilian labor force the economy has been experiencing since the middle of 1996 appears to have come to an end.
"We have two months back to back now in which the civilian labor force, over the two months as a whole, has declined by almost 150,000," Gramley said.
"And if we're back now to trend rates of growth of the civilian labor force, then growth of employment has to slow still more to avoid a still further drop in the unemployment rate," Gramley added.
Analysts said they do not expect the Fed to raise the federal funds rate by more than 25 basis points if the central bank indeed decides to tighten monetary policy in July.

The Fed last raised the federal funds rate on March 25, when it increased the rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The Fed decided to leave interest rates unchanged during the latest FOMC meeting, on May 20.
